name: Cantharidin solution

lead: Cantharidin is a blistering compound from blister beetles. Dermatologists apply it to molluscum bumps and warts so a blister lifts the lesion away.
The FDA approved the Ycanth formulation for molluscum in July 2023.

paras: It causes a controlled blister in the skin layer holding the lesion; the blister heals and the lesion goes with it, reportedly without scarring.
Pain, blisters and chemical burns can occur on skin. Swallowing it can cause serious kidney and gut damage. It is prescription and clinician-applied.

chain: Cantharidin applied to lesions by a clinician
Blister forms and lifts the lesion
angle.text: A clinician paints the solution on molluscum bumps or warts, a blister forms and the lesion lifts away, typically healing without scarring. People seek it to clear visible bumps cosmetically and avoid scraping or freezing.

lead: Cantharidin is a blistering agent made by blister beetles that dermatologists apply to skin to remove molluscum contagiosum bumps and warts.[1][2] It helps looks by clearing visible lesions, and the blister-and-lift approach is reported to heal without scarring.[1] A prescription topical, Ycanth (VP-102), was approved by the FDA in July 2023 for molluscum contagiosum.[1]

Cantharidin was first isolated in 1810 by Pierre Robiquet from the beetles once sold as 'Spanish fly'.[1] Its use against warts was studied by 1958.[1] Phase 3 trials of VP-102 in molluscum enrolled over 500 people, and phase 2 trials examined common and genital warts.[3][4][2]

paras: Approved use is treatment of molluscum contagiosum in patients aged 2 and older.[1] Dilute solutions have also been used for common warts, and VP-102 has been tested on genital warts.[1][5] Molluscum lesions often clear by themselves in six to twelve months, and people who treat them do so for cosmetic reasons or to prevent spread.[6]

Two phase 3 randomized trials (about 262 and 266 participants) tested cantharidin application in molluscum, and the FDA approval was based on two double-blind placebo-controlled trials.[1][3][4] A phase 2 trial of 56 patients examined cantharidin with occlusion on common warts, and a 105-patient placebo-controlled phase 2 study tested VP-102 on external genital warts.[2][5] Cantharidin-induced blisters are also used as a research model of skin inflammation.[7]

Topical effects include pain and blistering, and severe chemical burns can occur; lesions heal without scarring per the encyclopedia account.[1][6] Swallowing cantharidin can cause serious gastrointestinal and kidney damage and is fatal at high doses.[1]

Cantharides preparations were used from antiquity as aphrodisiacs and irritants, and Robiquet isolated the pure compound in 1810.[1] Verrica's Ycanth became the first FDA-approved molluscum treatment in 2023.[1]
